passage:
First week of April. Shreya heard it in the college canteen: two boys arguing in Assamese about a cricket match. She stopped with her tray in her hands. She hadn't spoken her own language out loud in Bengaluru for four months.
Bihu, mid-April. Her roommate Nazia found her on the hostel terrace at night, playing dhol videos on her phone, eyes wet. "Home's that good?" Shreya laughed. "In my head the lanes are always washed with rain, and Aita's pitha is always hot. Actually, the drain overflowed every year and I fought with my cousins all Bihu."
A week later. Over instant noodles, she taught Nazia three Assamese words, and felt, for an evening, a little less far away.

qa.a: Assamese.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling on the hostel terrace during Bihu?
qa.a: Shreya was homesick, aching for home, its festival, language and lanes, while knowing the memory was nicer than the real thing.

qa.a: Shreya taught Nazia three Assamese words, bringing a little of home into the present and feeling less far away.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel on finding Shreya on the terrace?
qa.a: Nazia may be touched and a bit worried, and curious about a home that clearly means so much to Shreya.

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage: Rajni, you're leaving for Chennai next week, so let your Vishal Chacha tell you something. I was nineteen when I went there for engineering. Nobody on my floor spoke Bhojpuri. I'd lie awake remembering the ghats at dawn, the bells, the smell of kachori from the lane behind our house, Dev Deepawali with lamps floating on the river. I missed it so much my chest hurt. When I finally came home that December, the lane was muddy, the kachori man had shut shop, and my brothers fought over the one fan. And I thought, the Banaras I missed was partly one I'd built in my head. Still, I missed it. You will too, beta. Let it ache a little. Then call home, and go eat idli.

qa.a: Chennai.

qa.q: What did Vishal Chacha realise on coming home that December?

qa.a: Letting it ache a little, then calling home and trying the local food, lets Rajni feel the longing without getting stuck in it.

qa.a: Rajni may feel reassured that missing home is normal, and closer to Vishal Chacha for sharing it. 🙂

subtype: Hiraeth for a home and language left behind [Actor]
passage: Navratri had begun in Darshan's town in Gujarat, and he was stuck in Pune with a practical exam on the fifth day and just enough money for mess fees. His mother sent a video: the chowk lit up, the garba circle spinning, his cousins in bright kediyus. Darshan played it three times in the hostel corridor, the only place with signal. He could almost smell the farsan stall. He forgot, for a moment, that last year he'd complained all nine nights about the loudspeakers keeping him awake. His roommate Madhav, from Nagpur, leaned out. "You're humming again." "Am I?" Darshan hadn't heard anyone speak Gujarati in three weeks. He answered his mother with a long voice note, in Gujarati, just to hear himself say the words.

passage: Ankita had imagined this visit for two years in her Hyderabad office cubicle: the mango orchard behind the school, the pond where she and Jyoti caught tadpoles, the tea shop where old Hari kaka played the radio. The bus dropped her at a new highway flyover. The orchard was a row of shops selling phone covers. The pond had been filled in for a petrol pump. Hari kaka's shop was now a cash machine. Jyoti was there, at least, waiting by the old banyan with a baby on her hip. They hugged, laughed, talked about nothing. It was lovely. But walking back, Ankita realised what she'd been missing wasn't really the pond. It was being twelve, with nowhere else to be.

passage: For three years in Toronto, Valentina had dreamed of the bakery on Via Roma in her grandmother's town in Sicily: warm bread at six in the morning, Nonna's hand in hers. She flew back in June and walked there first, with her friend Mei trailing jet-lagged behind. The bakery was a phone shop. Nonna's house had new owners and a satellite dish. The piazza where she'd learned to ride a bike was a car park. Mei touched her arm. "You okay?" Valentina nodded, then shook her head. "It's not even the bakery. It's that Nonna isn't here. And I'm not eight." They found another bakery two streets away. The bread was good. It wasn't the same, and it never would be.

passage: The principal's office at his old school in Shillong had new glass doors, and Alka Ma'am, now the principal, had grey in her hair. Bhupen, back for the first time since he left for Delhi at eighteen, sat opposite her with a cup of tea. "The old wooden block?" he asked. "Pulled down after the earthquake cracks. The new labs are there now." He walked the corridors afterwards. No creaking floor. No smell of wet raincoats and pine. The mural of the river they'd painted in Class 9 was under new paint. Only the bell sounded the same. He stood very still when it rang. It wasn't the building he'd been missing all those years in Delhi. It was the boy who ran to it.

subtype: Parent at home yearning for the grown child [Observer]
passage:
Saturday, home.
Came home for two days. Mummy had kept my room exactly as I left it three years ago: the blue bedsheet, my school trophies dusted, even my old hair clips in the drawer. My sister Sonali whispered that Mummy airs the room every Sunday and sits in there with her tea. Tonight I found Mummy in the hallway, stopped in front of my graduation photo, just looking. She didn't hear me. When she turned round, she smiled like nothing had happened and asked if I wanted more rice.
I've been calling every other week. Short calls. 'All fine, Mummy, busy.' I think those calls are her whole Sunday.
Calling on Wednesdays too from now on. Maybe video.
— Mehak

qa.q: How often does Mummy air the room, according to Sonali?
qa.a: Every Sunday.

qa.q: What might Mummy be feeling as she stands in front of the graduation photo?
qa.a: Mummy seems to be missing Mehak deeply, quietly waiting for a child who has grown up and moved away.

qa.a: Mehak decides to call on Wednesdays too, maybe by video, since even short calls clearly mean a great deal to Mummy.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about the extra Wednesday calls?
qa.a: Mummy would probably feel less alone in the waiting, and the calls might mean far more to her than the few words spoken. 🤍

At dinner Amma glanced at the door twice when the dog barked. Then the phone rang: Himani, a video call, the screen shaky. Amma didn't say much. 'Eating properly? Wearing warm clothes?' But she held the phone with both hands, close to her face, long after the talk had turned to nothing. When it ended, she sat in the dark a while. Sarita put a hand on her shoulder and said nothing.

Eid in Leeds was not like home, but it wasn't sad either, so don't worry.

Then I took the leftovers to the common room in my building. Wanjiru from Kenya, Tom from Wales and the Polish girls upstairs came. None of them had tasted sheer khurma. Tom had three bowls.
I'm keeping Hyderabad in my kitchen, Apa, and making a little home here too. Both fit.
Your Rehana

passage:
Sunday
I still can't sleep. Elizabeth and I went to watch the state women's hockey final at the stadium, our district against the champions. I don't even play hockey! But when it went to extra time, my heart was banging so hard I thought people could hear it. I bit the end of Elizabeth's dupatta. I actually prayed. When our striker scored in the last minute, the whole stand went up like one body, and I screamed words that aren't words. Elizabeth was crying. A lady behind us hugged us both.
On the bus home everybody was singing, even strangers. I didn't know you could feel that happy about something that wasn't even yours. Except it felt like ours.
— Salma

qa.q: Who hugged Salma and Elizabeth?
qa.a: The lady behind them hugged them both.

qa.q: Why did the win feel like "ours" to Salma, who doesn't even play hockey?
qa.a: Salma felt thrilled and connected to the team and the crowd, so the win felt personal, shared with everyone there.

qa.q: What could Salma choose to do to feel that shared joy again?
qa.a: Salma could go to more local matches with Elizabeth, or join a club, since being part of a crowd behind a team clearly lifts Salma's spirits.

qa.q: What might the win mean to the strangers singing on the bus?
qa.a: For them the win was a shared joy too, turning a bus full of people who didn't know each other into one celebrating group.

grounding: A teenager who doesn't play hockey feels a state final as if it were personal and shares the joy with a whole crowd.

subtype: Absorbing strangers' pain from the news feed [Actor]
passage: I'm Arnab, Gopika's cousin; we share a flat near the university. Something's been off with her this week. She comes back from classes and lies on the sofa scrolling through news about the floods up north: families on rooftops, a child crying, a man searching for his cattle. She watches them one after another, sometimes for two hours. She doesn't cry. She just gets quieter, and snappy if I talk. Last night she didn't eat, and at midnight she was still scrolling, jaw tight. When I asked what was wrong, she said, 'Nothing. I don't know. I just feel awful.' I can't tell what's going on inside her. But I made tea and asked if she wanted to walk to the canteen with me.

qa.q: What news has Gopika been scrolling through?
qa.a: News about the floods up north.

qa.q: What might Gopika's tight jaw and "I just feel awful" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Gopika is soaking up strangers' suffering without understanding why she feels so low, and has nowhere to put the feeling.

qa.q: What small step could help Gopika tonight?
qa.a: Arnab's offer of tea and a walk is a good start; Gopika could also put the phone away for the evening and later look for one small way to help.

qa.q: How is Arnab affected by watching this?
qa.a: Arnab seems worried and a little helpless, unsure what Gopika feels but gently trying to pull her away from the screen.

grounding: A cousin watches a young woman scroll flood news for hours, growing tense and low without knowing why.

subtype: Absorbing strangers' pain from the news feed [Actor]
passage:
Monday. Reena opened a news site on the metro and fell into a long thread about a building fire in another city: photos, voice notes, names. She got off two stops late. All afternoon her chest felt tight, and she snapped at Yusuf in the library for tapping his pen.
Thursday. She scrolled again before bed, then again at 2 a.m. Her stomach ached. She didn't know any of those people. She couldn't do anything. Why did she feel this bad?
The next Monday. Yusuf, noticing her dark circles, asked what was going on. She showed him her screen time. He whistled. 'Three hours of this, every day?' She hadn't realised. That evening she moved the news site off her home screen and called her mother instead.

qa.q: How many stops late did Reena get off on Monday?
qa.a: Two stops late.

qa.q: What was Reena thinking on Thursday night?
qa.a: Reena was puzzled why she felt so bad about strangers she couldn't help, as their pain seemed to soak in anyway.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Reena choose to do?
qa.a: Seeing the screen time with Yusuf was the turning point; Reena then moved the news site off the home screen and called her mother.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt being snapped at on Monday?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt confused or hurt at first, but later noticed Reena's dark circles and cared enough to ask.

grounding: Over a week, a student absorbs a fire tragedy through hours of scrolling, feels tense and low without knowing why, then changes her habit.

subtype: Absorbing strangers' pain from the news feed [Actor]
passage: Nikita, you look like I did at twenty. Let me tell you something. The year I started college, there was a terrible earthquake far away, and our hostel TV showed it day and night. I sat in front of it for hours every evening. Fallen houses, a mother calling a name. I didn't know anyone there. I couldn't send anything; I had forty rupees for the month. But I stopped sleeping properly. I got angry at silly things, cried in the bathroom, and couldn't say why. My warden finally switched off the TV and said, 'Tanuja, feeling their pain is not the same as helping them.' She took me to pack relief bundles at the church hall. My hands felt useful again. So, beta, put that phone down for a while.

qa.q: How much money did Tanuja have for the month?
qa.a: Forty rupees.

qa.q: Why did young Tanuja get angry and cry without being able to say why?
qa.a: Tanuja had been soaking up strangers' pain from the TV for hours with no way to help, and the helpless feeling built up inside.

qa.q: What did the warden choose to do, and why did it help?
qa.a: The warden switched off the TV and took Tanuja to pack relief bundles, turning helpless feeling into something useful.

qa.q: Why might Tanuja be telling Nikita this story now?
qa.a: Tanuja seems to see Nikita absorbing distressing news on the phone, and wants to spare Nikita the same helpless heaviness.

grounding: An elder recalls absorbing earthquake news for hours at twenty, feeling low and angry without knowing why, when there was nothing to be done.

subtype: Feeling with others without taking the feeling over [Response]
passage: The fire at the cloth market in Nagaur had taken seven shops, including Zubin's father's. Ritu, who taught Zubin in Class 8, heard the whole story from him at the school gate: the smoke, his father sitting on the kerb all night. Walking home, her own chest felt tight, her eyes hot. At home she sat on the charpai, breathed slowly, and said it to herself: this is their loss, not mine. I can feel for them without carrying all of it. She switched off the TV news about the fire and made tea. Then she did one small thing. Next morning she went round the staff room collecting spare notebooks and a school bag, since Zubin's books had burned with the shop. She handed them over quietly, and went back to teaching.

qa.q: How many shops did the fire take?
qa.a: Seven shops.

qa.q: Why did Ritu tell herself "this is their loss, not mine"?
qa.a: Ritu felt the family's pain as a tight chest and hot eyes, and wanted to care for them without being overwhelmed by feelings that weren't hers.

qa.q: What small act did Ritu choose, and why did it suit the situation?
qa.a: Ritu collected notebooks and a school bag, since Zubin's books had burned; it turned her concern into practical help.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel receiving the notebooks and bag?
qa.a: Zubin would likely feel cared for and a little less weighed down, able to keep up at school after the fire.

grounding: A teacher shaken by a student's family losing their shop separates their grief from her own, takes a break from the news, and gathers school supplies.

subtype: Feeling with others without taking the feeling over [Response]
passage: Wei had spent Sunday morning reading about the earthquake overseas, photo after photo, until her coffee went cold and her shoulders were up by her ears. Her sister Xin found her still on the couch at noon. 'You look like you were there.' Wei put the phone face down. She noticed the tightness in her chest and named it quietly: this is their grief, not mine. I can care without drowning in it. She set a rule: news once a day, briefly, then off. That evening she signed up for Saturdays at the community centre in Vancouver, sorting donated winter coats for newly arrived families. The first Saturday, her arms ached from lifting boxes. Her chest didn't.

qa.q: What did Wei sign up to do on Saturdays?
qa.a: Sort donated winter coats for newly arrived families at the community centre.

qa.q: What did Wei feel and realise on putting the phone down?
qa.a: Wei noticed a tightness in her chest and recognised she was taking on grief that belonged to others.

qa.q: Which of Wei's choices made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Turning the feeling into Saturday volunteering gave the care somewhere to go, so Wei ended up tired in the arms but lighter in the chest.

qa.q: How might Xin see the change in Wei after that Sunday?
qa.a: Xin, who said Wei looked like she'd been there, would probably be relieved to see Wei calmer and doing something useful.

grounding: An adult notices she is absorbing distant disaster news, limits her viewing, and channels the feeling into volunteering.

subtype: Feeling with others without taking the feeling over [Response]
passage: At the hospital billing desk, Aparna heard hard stories all day: a father counting notes twice, a daughter asking how long the room would cost, a woman crying quietly into her dupatta. By Wednesday her own stomach was in knots every evening. So she changed a few things. Between patients, she took one slow breath and told herself: their fear, not mine; my job is to be steady for them. At lunch she walked round the hospital garden instead of eating at the counter. And she asked Akash, her supervisor, if she could make a simple one-page sheet in Hindi and English explaining the charity fund and whom to ask. Akash said yes. On Friday, when the father came back, she handed him the sheet before he even asked.

qa.q: Where did Aparna walk at lunch?
qa.a: Round the hospital garden.

qa.q: What did Aparna want when telling herself "their fear, not mine"?
qa.a: Aparna wanted to stay caring but steady, without taking on every family's fear as her own.

qa.q: Why was the one-page sheet a good use of Aparna's feelings?
qa.a: It turned concern into a small, practical help, so families could find the charity fund without extra worry.

qa.q: How might the father feel receiving the sheet before asking?
qa.a: The father would probably feel relieved and respected, noticed without having to explain his worry again.

grounding: A hospital billing worker steadies herself against families' distress, takes breaks, and makes a help sheet for them.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage: From my balcony I saw it happen. Jomon, from the ground floor, fell off the swing and landed hard on the gravel. He lay there crying, holding his knee. Seema, his little playmate, was right beside him. She didn't go to him or call anyone. She just stood with her fists clenched and screamed, louder than Jomon, tears pouring, frozen to the spot. She looked as frightened as if she had fallen herself. By the time I ran down, both were sobbing. I picked Jomon up and held Seema's hand. After a while she whispered, 'Is he broken?'

qa.q: Where did Jomon land?
qa.a: Hard on the gravel.

qa.q: What does Seema's whisper "Is he broken?" suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Seema cared about Jomon deeply but was so frightened that she couldn't move or help.

qa.q: What could an adult teach Seema for the next time a friend gets hurt?
qa.a: An adult could practise a simple plan with Seema, like taking a big breath and running to call a grown-up, so the caring can turn into help.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt with Seema screaming beside him?
qa.a: Jomon may have felt even more scared, with his friend crying louder and nobody coming until the neighbour ran down.

grounding: A neighbour sees a five-year-old freeze and scream when her friend falls, too distressed to help though she cares.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage:
Monday. At the park, Parveen tripped on the slide steps and cut her chin. Imran, five, burst into tears and stood rooted, hands over his eyes, while Parveen cried alone until her Nani came running.
Wednesday. At bedtime Imran told Ammi, 'I didn't help Parveen. I was crying too much.' His lip shook. Ammi hugged him. 'You felt very sad for her. That shows you care.'
Saturday. Imran took Parveen a lion sticker. 'For your chin,' he said, and she let him touch the plaster.

qa.q: Where did Parveen cut herself?
qa.a: On her chin, tripping on the slide steps.

qa.q: How did Imran feel on Wednesday about what happened?
qa.a: Imran felt guilty and sad for not helping, because he had been crying too much to move.

qa.q: After the hug, what could Ammi teach Imran for next time?
qa.a: Ammi could practise a simple step with Imran, like shouting for a grown-up, so the caring can turn into help even when he feels scared.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel receiving the lion sticker?
qa.a: Parveen would probably feel cared for and happy, seeing that Imran was still thinking about her chin.

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old too upset to help a hurt friend shows his care later with a sticker.

subtype: Child freezes and cries at a friend's fall [Actor]
passage: The wedding band was so loud that nobody heard Gautam fall. He and Jaya, both five, had been racing up the wet marble steps behind the lawn when his sandal slipped and he banged his elbow. He sat howling. Jaya stopped dead. Her face crumpled, and she screamed too, frozen on the step, fists at her sides. Her legs wouldn't move. The dhol drowned them both. It was a long minute before Gautam's uncle, looking for more sweets, spotted them and ran over. He picked up Gautam and held out a hand to Jaya. She clung to it, sobbing, 'He fell, he fell.'

qa.q: What drowned out the children's crying?
qa.a: The dhol.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling when her legs wouldn't move?
qa.a: Jaya was overwhelmed by fear for Gautam; she cared, but her own upset froze her.

qa.q: Once the fright has passed, what could an adult do with Jaya?
qa.a: An adult could praise Jaya's caring and practise what to do next time, like running to find a grown-up, which is hard to think of when frightened.

qa.q: How might Gautam's uncle see Jaya's screaming?
qa.a: The uncle might realise Jaya was frightened for Gautam rather than hurt, which is why he held out a hand to her too.

grounding: At a noisy wedding, a five-year-old freezes and screams when her friend falls, too overwhelmed to fetch help.
